newsitem.title: USA: Supreme Court upholds USDA generic ad program.
newsitem.headline: Supreme Court upholds USDA generic ad program.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday upheld a federal programme that requires California fruit growers to chip in for industrywide, generic advertising campaigns, saying it was not a violation of free speech rights.
The high court, by a 5-4 vote, reversed an appeals court ruling that the assessments were unconstitutional.

Under an agricultural marketing law born in the New Deal era, producers and distributors of California peaches, plums and nectarines are required to contribute for generic advertisements, such as "Eat a California peach."
Assessments are based on a charge for each box of fruit marketed. The programme generates about $14 million to $15 million per year for advertising and promotion.

A decade ago, a group of growers led by family-owned Wileman Bros & Elliott, of Cutler, Calif., challenged the marketing requirement, claiming a First Amendment right to not take part in government-compelled speech.

The Agriculture Department defended the programme, saying the fees were like union dues and that the advertising boosted sales. It also argued that mandatory assessments were necessary to prevent growers from getting a "free ride" from commercials funded by other producers.
A U.S. Court of Appeals ruling in 1995 sided with the growers. The Clinton Administration petitioned the Supreme Court.
Justice John Paul Stevens said for the court majority that the requirement did not violate the First Amendment.

"The mere fact that one or more producers 'do not wish to foster' generic advertising of their product is not a sufficient reason for overriding the judgment of the majority of market participants, bureaucrats, and legislators who have concluded that such programmes are beneficial," he wrote.

For the dissent, Justice David Souter wrote: "...forced payment for commercial speech should be subject to the same level of judicial scrutiny as any restriction on communications in that category. Because I believe that the advertising scheme here fails that test, I respectfully dissent."
The decision is a huge victory for the Agriculture Department which runs about 29 similiar marketing programmes across the nation for produce ranging from watermelon to beef.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman applauded the High Court ruling, saying it validated USDA's marketing programmes.

"These generic commodity promotion programmes have been a mainstay for the agriculture industry and consumers for more than half a century," he said. "As the majority of producers have found, product promotion tools increase sales, both at home and in international markets."
